This table summarizes the progression of tutorial concepts from Week 1 to Week 6 across **Coding**, **Collaboration**, and **Automation**. Each bullet gives a quick explanation of the concept.

| Week | Coding (R, SQL) | Collaboration (Git, GitHub) | Automation (README, Make) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Week 1 — Foundations** | • **R and Positron** — R runs the analysis; Positron is an IDE for writing code and inspecting results.<br>• **Projects and paths** — Keep related files together and use project-relative paths so work can move between computers.<br>• **Objects and data types** — Vectors and data frames hold values; logical values and missing data need interpretation.<br>• **Import and inspect** — Read a CSV, check its rows, columns, types, and basic summaries before analyzing it.<br>• **`dplyr` and pipes** — Select, filter, create, group, summarize, sort, and count data in a readable sequence. | • **Git and GitHub** — Git records project history locally; GitHub hosts repositories and supports collaboration.<br>• **Repository and commit** — A repository holds tracked files; a commit records a named snapshot of staged changes.<br>• **Basic workflow** — Use `status`, `add`, `commit`, and `push` to inspect, record, and share work.<br>• **Local and remote copies** — Your local repository is on your computer; the remote is the shared hosted copy. | • **ITO workflow** — Organize scripts around setup, input, transformation, and output.<br>• **Run a script** — `Rscript analysis.R` runs saved work from the terminal in a repeatable order.<br>• **Reproducibility** — Scripts record steps so the same analysis can be rerun and inspected. |
| **Week 2 — Documents and project workflow** | • **Quarto, Markdown, and R Markdown** — Combine narrative, code, and results in a document that can be rendered.<br>• **YAML and chunks** — YAML sets document options; code chunks run analysis in document order.<br>• **Data audit** — Identify the unit of observation, inspect missingness, and assess whether values make sense.<br>• **Cleaning and derived measures** — Filter and rename variables, handle dates and factors, and calculate new summaries. | • **Explore and copy projects** — Browse a repository, clone it to your computer, or fork a separate GitHub copy.<br>• **Sync work** — Pull remote changes before continuing and push commits to share your work.<br>• **Issues and boards** — Track tasks on a lightweight board such as backlog, to do, in progress, and done.<br>• **`.gitignore`** — Keep generated, private, or machine-specific files out of Git tracking. | • **README** — Tell collaborators the project goal, required data and software, run steps, and expected outputs.<br>• **Render reports** — Use `quarto render report.qmd` to rebuild a report from its source.<br>• **One source of truth** — Keep code and explanation together so outputs can be refreshed when data change. |
| **Week 3 — Visualization and Make basics** | • **Grammar of graphics** — Choose data, map variables in `aes()`, and add a geometry for how to draw them.<br>• **Choose a plot** — Points show relationships; lines show ordered trends; bars compare categories; histograms show distributions.<br>• **Compare distributions** — Boxplots summarize median and spread; violin plots show distribution shape.<br>• **Improve a figure** — Use labels, themes, facets, colors, transparency, and `ggsave()` to make plots readable. | • **Branches** — Create a separate line of work while keeping `main` stable.<br>• **Pull request review** — Inspect commits and the red/green diff before proposing changes for merge.<br>• **Merge and cleanup** — Merge an approved PR and delete its finished branch.<br>• **History and recovery** — Use commit logs and deliberate conflict resolution to understand or restore earlier work. | • **Make rules** — A target names an output, prerequisites name its inputs, and a recipe builds it.<br>• **Recipe syntax** — Make recipes begin with a tab; the first ordinary target is the default goal.<br>• **Preview dependencies** — `make -n` previews commands without running them; complete prerequisites let Make detect changes.<br>• **Phony targets** — Names such as `all` and `clean` are commands, not files; declare them with `.PHONY`. |
| **Week 4 — Data engineering workflow** | • **Feature engineering** — Use `mutate()`, `rank()`, `case_when()`, and `distinct()` to create and audit variables.<br>• **Grouped summaries** — Change the unit of analysis by counting and calculating totals, means, medians, or other statistics per group.<br>• **Keys and joins** — Choose matching identifiers and a join type; repeated keys can multiply rows.<br>• **Time-aware data** — Parse timestamps, aggregate by day, and use `lag()` to compare with a previous period. | • **Small commits** — Record focused changes with messages that describe the work.<br>• **Separate branches** — Isolate data work from automation work to make review clearer.<br>• **Multiple PRs** — Review, merge, and clean up separate feature branches; inspect history and diffs. | • **Modular scripts** — Split preparation and reporting into small steps with clear inputs and outputs.<br>• **Data folders** — Keep raw inputs unchanged, intermediate outputs separate, and final deliverables in an output location.<br>• **Clean rebuild** — Remove generated files with a deliberate clean rule, then rebuild from source inputs and code. |
| **Week 5 — Advanced preparation, SQL, and pipelines** | • **Clean text** — Use regular expressions with `grepl()` to detect patterns and `gsub()` to replace text.<br>• **Reshape data** — `pivot_longer()` gathers columns into rows; `pivot_wider()` spreads values into columns.<br>• **Time series** — Use ISO weeks, complete expected key/date grids, create trends, and compare periods with `lag()` or `lead()`.<br>• **Missing values** — LOCF assumes a value stays stable; interpolation assumes smooth change. Choose based on the variable.<br>• **SQL and SQLite** — Query relational tables with `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, joins, and `ORDER BY`.<br>• **Structured formats** — JSON can hold nested records; inspect and preserve structure before flattening it. | • **Continue source control** — Apply the established branch and commit workflow to source-code changes.<br>• **Separate code and outputs** — Commit scripts and documentation rather than generated datasets. | • **Full pipeline** — Connect preparation, analysis, and reporting targets into a single build.<br>• **Build and clean** — Use `all`, `clean`, dry runs, and rebuilds to check a pipeline.<br>• **Scale the Makefile** — Use Make variables, modular folders, and nested Makefiles for larger workflows. |
| **Week 6 — AI-assisted and repeated analysis** | • **Prompting** — Specify task, context, constraints, output, and checks; the analyst defines research measures.<br>• **Agent-assisted coding** — Use an agent to inspect files, run R or SQL, and propose code changes.<br>• **Repeated analysis** — Use `split()` and `lapply()` for per-creator plots and regressions; interpret synthetic results as associations, not causal effects.<br>• **Verify exports** — Check columns, row counts, key uniqueness, and output files, not just whether a script ran. | • **Bound permissions** — Specify which files and commands an agent may use, plus when it must stop and ask.<br>• **Review changes** — Inspect the agent's plan, actions, file diff, and test results before accepting them.<br>• **Protect project assets** — Keep API keys and sensitive data out of prompts and tracked files. | • **Agent-built Makefile** — Ask for a small workflow using existing files and explicit dependencies.<br>• **Check the build** — Preview with `make -n`, build, rerun to confirm no work is needed, then clean and rebuild.<br>• **Agent or pipeline?** — Agents choose actions from observations; Make follows the repeatable rules you define. |
